newsitem.title: UK: British royals "encouraged" after TV poll boost.
newsitem.headline: British royals "encouraged" after TV poll boost.

text.p: Britain's scandal-ridden royal family were "encouraged" on Wednesday by a phone-in poll giving two-to-one backing for the monarchy, Buckingham Palace said.

But heir-to-the-throne Prince Charles received a warning about his own standing following his acrimonious divorce from Princess Diana last year and his adulterous affair with old flame Camilla Parker Bowles.

Of more than 2.6 million callers to Independent Television during a studio debate broadcast live on Tuesday evening, 66 percent voted to retain the royal family and 34 percent said it should be scrapped.
It was Britain's largest television opinion poll and the studio audience of 3,000 people from around the country was also the country's biggest ever, organisers said.

Despite the support for the royal family, commentators said the exercise had cheapened the 1,000-year monarchy. "Rationality is dethroned as television debates and deflates the monarchy," said a headline in The Times.
The studio debate was widely criticised as rowdy, ill-informed and bad-tempered. Royalists said they were frozen out of the discussion in favour of republicans.
The Evening Standard said: "If this was what the popular will looked like, then perhaps an autocratic sovereign wasn't such a bad idea."
Sir Bernard Ingham, who was Margaret Thatcher's press secretary when she was prime minister, described the debate as a disgrace. "It was a sort of a pub brawl at times," he said.
A Buckingham palace spokesman said: "The quality of debate last night left something to be desired. It was more entertainment than a real opportunity for serious discussion."

But he added: "It was encouraging that there was so much interest in the issues and, after the difficulties of recent years, that so many people took the trouble to show their support for the monarchy."
But the debate held a clear message for Prince Charles.
Studio audience members were given cards -- blue for yes and red for no -- to vote on questions put to them during the course of the discussion.
When they were asked if Charles should become king in succession to his mother, Queen Elizabeth, with Camilla as queen, the huge auditorium turned into a sea of red.

As the debate was being held, Prince Charles returned to London after a skiing holiday during which he was reported to have told friends that he had failed the British monarchy and vowed to "sort the whole bloody mess out" by reaching out more to ordinary people.
Charles's public standing plummetted during the bitter break-up of his 15-year marriage and his confession of an extra-marital affair with Camilla Parker Bowles.
Charles is believed to want to mend fences, at least in public, with the popular Princess Diana, the mother of Prince William, 14, and 12-year-old Prince Harry.
"I've done a lot of things wrong and I've been doing so for too long," Monday's Daily Mirror quoted him as admitting to friends.
"I've let the queen down, my family -- including William and Harry -- and Camilla. I've let down the whole institution of the monarchy. I've even failed Diana."
Charles has also signalled he wants to play a greater role in the Church of England, of which he will be head when he succeeds the throne, toning down remarks in favour of other religions.
